transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-16
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Samir (Redwood Solutions), Priya (Lakeland CTO), Ethan (Lakeland ML), Liam (Lakeland PM)

Auto-summary (auto gen, may be rough): Quick hosted API walkthrough, streaming demo, showed parameter effects and how to do retries safely. Customer asked about data retention, KMS, and whether streaming costs more.

[00:00] Maya: Hi everyone thanks for joining, this is Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE, with me is Carlos our SE who will walk through the hosted API chat and text generation basics.
[00:10] Priya: Hey Maya thanks, excited to see the demo. We want to evaluate hosted first, cost and latency are the big things for us.
[00:18] Carlos: great, quick agenda - we'll show the basic chat API, streaming responses, common params (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), and then best practices for retries and idempotency. we'll also hit on security briefly.
[00:28] Ethan: quick context - we run a customer support summarization pipeline, about 150k msgs/day, 99th p95 latency target for single-turn summarization is ~200ms for the edge cases.
[00:40] Maya: good to know. so hosted API is usually the fastest path to get started, we have models tuned for cost/latency tradeoffs, and you can pin versions. if you later need dedicated capacity we can move you there with same API.
[00:55] Liam: question - is streaming more expensive? like if we open a socket and stream tokens does that increase cost?
[01:05] Carlos: good question - pricing is per-token regardless of streaming vs non-streaming. streaming improves perceived latency because you get tokens earlier, but total token count similar. small overhead for extra network calls if you do a lot of tiny chunks but that's negligible.
[01:20] Priya: okay, and what about retries? we have flaky upstream network occasionally and want to avoid double-charging or double side-effects.
[01:30] Carlos: for idempotent generation calls we recommend including an idempotency_key header on requests; if the request fails you can safely retry with exponential backoff. for streaming specifically, the client should re-establish stream and resume or restart - we provide a short TTL to accept idempotent retries. i'll show an example.
[01:46] (Carlos shares screen, shows a code snippet)
[01:50] Carlos: here's a minimal curl example and a node snippet. reminder the params: temperature controls randomness (0-1), top_p does nucleus sampling, max_tokens limits the generation length, and stop sequences you can set to truncate.
[02:05] Carlos: // pseudo code
fetch('/v1/chat', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { Authorization: 'Bearer <key>', 'Idempotency-Key': '<uuid>' },
  body: { model: 'rw-medium-1', messages: [...], temperature: 0.2, top_p: 0.9, max_tokens: 256, stream: true }
})
[02:30] Maya: note - rw-medium-1 is an example from our catalog, we show perf numbers in the docs. small models are cheaper and lower-latency but if you need high-quality hallucination-resistance we recommend the larger family.
[02:45] Ethan: latency numbers? p95?
[02:48] Carlos: for hosted in us-west with rw-medium-1 single-turn, p95 is typically ~120-250ms depending on prompt length. we have benchmarks per model and per sequence length in the console. these are verified but your workload can vary - recommend running a small benchmark test.
[03:05] Priya: what about prefix caching or KV cache? we do a lot of similar contexts across customers.
[03:12] Carlos: yes, we support prefix caching and automatic KV cache reuse in the runtime. it's enabled at the route level and reduces repeated compute for the same prefix. sometimes transcription of our docs says \"K V cash\" but it's KV cache.
[03:22] Liam: haha noted. can you demo streaming?
[03:25] Carlos: sure - i'll kick off a sample chat with stream:true and show tokens arriving in the console.
[03:32] [03:32] Carlos: (starts stream) token: "Hello" ... token: "thank you for reaching out" ... the client receives deltas as they're produced. if you want to show typing indicator UI you can render partial fragments.
[03:50] Ethan: if we get a 5xx mid-stream, do we resume? get duplicate tokens?
[03:55] Carlos: if a 5xx occurs, the safe approach is to retry using the same idempotency key after waiting. if partial output was delivered, you may need to dedupe on your side by comparing final response ids. we also offer response IDs in the response metadata.
[04:12] Priya: security questions - data retention, encryption at rest, KMS, and SSO for our engineers.
[04:20] Maya: good - we retain logs per customer policy; hosted by default keeps request/response short-term but can be turned off for enterprise. we support customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM for encrypting stored artifacts and SSO via SAML/SCIM, RBAC in the console.
[04:35] Ethan: can we bring our own KMS?
[04:37] Carlos: yes, we integrate with customer KMS for Private and Dedicated; for hosted we have a customer-managed keys option for enterprise accounts - i'll share the integration doc.
[04:45] (Priya types)
[04:48] Priya: any compliance certs? SOC2?
[04:50] Maya: yes SOC2 Type II, and we have ISO roadmapped; i'll attach the SOC2 report.
[04:57] Carlos: also for data residency we can pin region routing and keep data in specific cloud regions.
[05:05] Liam: back to retry behaviour - do you recommend client-level exponential backoff?
[05:10] Carlos: yes, typical pattern is exponential backoff with jitter and max 3 retries for idempotent calls. for non-idempotent or side-effectful calls, implement server-side dedupe or use a job queue to make the generation request once.
[05:23] Maya: i'll drop a sample retry snippet in the follow-up notes.
[05:27] Carlos: (shows SDK snippet) const res = await client.chat.stream({ model:'rw-small', messages, idempotency_key, retry:{retries:3, backoff:'exponential'} });
[05:40] Ethan: do you support streaming via websockets or SSE?
[05:43] Carlos: both. we support SSE and websockets for streaming; SSE is simplest for web UIs, websockets for two-way. We also support chunked HTTP streaming.
[05:53] Priya: question on function calling / structured output - does streaming support JSON-safe outputs? we need deterministic parseable JSON for some flows.
[06:03] Carlos: yes we have function-calling style structured outputs. when you require strict JSON we recommend using function call mode - the model returns a JSON payload and you can validate schemas. streaming and function calling can be combined but you need to handle partial payload assembly on client side.
[06:18] (brief demo: show function call payload returned)
[06:28] Maya: quick note on params tuning - lower temperature and lower top_p reduce variance and hallucinations; higher max_tokens obviously increases cost. we often recommend starting with temp 0.0-0.3 for summarization.
[06:43] Ethan: for summarization we also want to chunk long docs; any helper functions?
[06:47] Carlos: yes we have guidance in the docs and client helpers for chunking + context windows. also recommend using the console to test token counts so you can estimate cost.
[06:59] Liam: can we see a cost example: 150k msgs/day * avg 60 tokens out?
[07:05] Maya: we'll include a sample cost calc in the pricing doc - roughly tokens * model rate. Carlos will put a few scenarios for small/medium/large model choices.
[07:15] Priya: network egress to our app also matters - do you have recommendations to reduce latency?
[07:21] Carlos: route requests to the nearest region, enable TLS session reuse, and use the streaming client to show early tokens. also pin models to a region to avoid cross-region hops.
[07:34] (15 minute mark they deep dive a bit on model selection and show console dashboards)
[07:40] Carlos: showing console: route-level dashboards, latency breakdown by tokenization and generation, per-route cost. you can set alerts for quality regressions tied to eval prompt sets.
[07:55] Priya: any throttling/quotas we should worry about on hosted?
[07:59] Maya: hosted has rate limits but they are adjustable; for production scale we recommend Dedicated if you need guaranteed throughput. hosted is fine for most early-to-mid scale apps.
[08:08] Ethan: SLA on hosted?
[08:10] Maya: hosted has best-effort at standard tiers; enterprise plan includes SLAs and uptime guarantees - we'll include specifics in the enterprise pack.
[08:20] Liam: ok let's talk POC next steps, timeline.
[08:24] Priya: we want a 2-week pilot with realistic load and our prompts. can Redwood give trial keys and run a short benchmark?
[08:31] Maya: yes we can provision trial API keys and a small credit, Carlos will help set up benchmark tests and show how to run the SDK.
[08:38] Carlos: i'll need sample prompt sets and an estimate of typical request size. that helps pick model/region and batching configs.
[08:44] Ethan: i'll send 3 prompt types and a dataset size, plus expected concurrency.
[08:48] (small talk about metrics and instrumentation)
[08:55] Priya: one more question - do you store prompts for eval and how long?
[08:59] Maya: by default we store short-term for debugging and quality, but enterprise can opt-out; we can also route logs to your S3 via syslog, or disable retention.
[09:12] Carlos: ok wrapping up - recap of action items, we'll send SOC2, KMS docs, pricing, provision trial keys, and schedule POC scoping.
[09:25] Priya: sounds good, thanks for the demo.
[09:28] Maya: thanks all.
